name: British Expansion in India – Bengal, Anglo-Maratha Wars & Subsidiary Alliance System

notes.heading: Overview
points: British expansion in India began with control over Bengal after 1757
It was followed by systematic conquest of Maratha territories
Diplomatic tools like Subsidiary Alliance helped in indirect expansion
Company rule shifted from trade to territorial control
By early 19th century, British became dominant power in India

notes.heading: British Expansion in Bengal – Background
points: Bengal was the richest province of Mughal Empire
Known for textiles, agriculture, and revenue surplus
Decline of Mughal authority allowed Bengal Nawabs to gain autonomy
British East India Company established strong trading base in Bengal
Conflicts arose between Nawabs and Company over trade privileges

notes.heading: Battle of Plassey (1757)
points: Fought between Siraj-ud-Daulah and British under Robert Clive
British victory due to conspiracy and support of Mir Jafar
Marked beginning of British political control in India
Company gained right to collect revenue in Bengal
Siraj-ud-Daulah was defeated and killed

notes.heading: Battle of Buxar (1764)
points: Fought between British and combined forces of Bengal, Awadh, and Mughal emperor
British led by Hector Munro
Decisive victory for British East India Company
Treaty of Allahabad (1765) granted Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa
Established Company as major political power in India

notes.heading: Significance of Bengal Conquest
points: Provided massive revenue base to British
Strengthened financial position of East India Company
Enabled further expansion in India
Bengal became center of British administration
Marked transition from trade to territorial empire

notes.heading: Anglo-Maratha Wars – Overview
points: Three major wars fought between British and Marathas (1775–1818)
Resulted in gradual decline of Maratha power
British used diplomacy, alliances, and military force
Maratha confederacy lacked unity
End of wars led to British dominance in India

notes.heading: First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–1782)
points: Fought due to internal Maratha succession disputes
British supported Raghunath Rao (Raghoba)
Ended with Treaty of Salbai (1782)
Restored status quo but increased British influence
Showed Maratha weakness in internal unity

notes.heading: Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–1805)
points: Fought during rule of Peshwa Baji Rao II
British under Lord Wellesley used Subsidiary Alliance system
Major battles at Assaye and Laswari
British gained control over Delhi, Agra, and large parts of central India
Maratha power significantly weakened

notes.heading: Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–1818)
points: Final conflict between British and Marathas
Led to complete defeat of Maratha Confederacy
Peshwa Baji Rao II was defeated and pensioned off
Abolition of Maratha political power
British established direct control over most of India

notes.heading: Subsidiary Alliance System – Introduction
points: Introduced by Lord Wellesley in 1798
Designed to bring Indian states under British control without direct annexation
Indian rulers had to accept British troops in their territory
States had to pay for maintenance of British forces
Rulers could not maintain independent foreign relations

notes.heading: Conditions of Subsidiary Alliance
points: Acceptance of British forces in the state
Payment of subsidy or surrender of territory
Appointment of British Resident in court
No alliances with other powers without British approval
Disbandment of independent army in some cases

notes.heading: States under Subsidiary Alliance
points: Hyderabad (first to accept system)
Mysore after defeat of Tipu Sultan
Awadh (Oudh)
Peshwa of Marathas
Many Rajput states

notes.heading: Impact of Subsidiary Alliance
points: Reduced sovereignty of Indian rulers
Increased British political control without annexation
Created financial burden on Indian states
Weakened native military forces
Expanded British Empire indirectly

notes.heading: British Expansion Strategy
points: Combination of war, diplomacy, and treaties
Exploitation of internal conflicts in Indian states
Use of superior military organization
Control over key revenue-rich regions like Bengal
Gradual territorial consolidation across India

notes.heading: Historical Significance
points: Bengal conquest provided financial base for empire
Anglo-Maratha wars eliminated major Indian power
Subsidiary Alliance enabled indirect colonial expansion
British became dominant political force in India
Foundation laid for British Raj in 19th century

name: Second Phase of British Expansion in India – Conquest of Sindh & Anglo-Sikh Wars

notes.heading: Overview
points: Second phase of British expansion focused on consolidating control over remaining independent regions
Sindh and Punjab were key targets due to strategic location
British used diplomacy, treaties, and military force for expansion
This phase marked final stages of territorial conquest in India
By mid-19th century, British dominance over India was almost complete

notes.heading: Second Phase of British Expansion – Background
points: After Bengal and Maratha conquest, British turned to north-west India
Strategic importance of Sindh and Punjab increased due to Afghan frontier
Fear of Russian expansion (Great Game) influenced British policy
Railways, trade routes, and military considerations played role
Doctrine of expansion became more aggressive under Dalhousie

notes.heading: Conquest of Sindh – Background
points: Sindh was ruled by Amirs (Talpur rulers)
Strategically important due to Indus River and trade routes
British interest increased due to fear of Russian influence via Afghanistan
Initially British signed treaties with Sindh rulers
Gradual interference led to annexation

notes.heading: Conquest of Sindh – Events
points: Treaty of 1832 allowed British trade navigation rights on Indus
Sir Charles Napier led military campaign against Sindh
Battle of Miani (1843) – British defeated Amirs of Sindh
Battle of Hyderabad (1843) – final defeat of Sindh rulers
Sindh annexed to British Empire in 1843

notes.heading: Significance of Sindh Conquest
points: Opened Indus river for British trade and military movement
Strengthened British north-west frontier control
Provided strategic base for Afghanistan policy
Extended British territorial dominance in western India
Set precedent for aggressive annexation policies

notes.heading: Anglo-Sikh Wars – Background
points: Punjab was ruled by powerful Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh
After his death (1839), empire became weak and unstable
Power struggles among Sikh chiefs and army (Khalsa) increased
British viewed Punjab as strategic buffer state
Tension between Sikh Empire and British increased

notes.heading: First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–1846)
points: Fought between Sikh Empire and British East India Company
Causes included political instability and Khalsa army expansion
Major battles: Mudki, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, Sobraon
Sikh forces defeated due to internal divisions
Treaty of Lahore (1846) signed after war

notes.heading: Results of First Anglo-Sikh War
points: British gained control over some Sikh territories
Sikh Empire weakened but not fully annexed
Jammu and Kashmir sold to Gulab Singh under Treaty of Amritsar
British Resident appointed in Lahore
Punjab remained unstable

notes.heading: Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848–1849)
points: Caused by rebellion in Multan and growing Sikh resentment
Sikh forces led by Sher Singh and others
Major battles: Ramnagar, Chillianwala, Gujrat
Battle of Gujrat (1849) decisive British victory
Led to complete annexation of Punjab in 1849

notes.heading: Significance of Anglo-Sikh Wars
points: End of independent Sikh Empire
Completion of British territorial expansion in North India
Punjab became British province
Strengthened British north-west frontier
Opened route for Central Asian strategic interests

notes.heading: Policy of Lord Dalhousie
points: Aggressive annexation policy in 1840s–1850s
Used Doctrine of Lapse in other regions (contextual link)
Focused on strategic consolidation
Annexed Sindh and Punjab during his tenure
Strengthened administrative control of Company

notes.heading: Causes of British Success
points: Superior military organization and discipline
Better artillery and logistics
Internal divisions in Indian states
Efficient intelligence and diplomacy
Strong financial and administrative backing

notes.heading: Historical Significance
points: Second phase completed British territorial expansion in India
Sindh and Punjab were final major annexations
British control extended to north-west frontier
India became fully integrated under Company rule
Prepared ground for direct Crown rule after 1857

name: Doctrine of Lapse & Annexation of Oudh

notes.heading: Overview
points: Doctrine of Lapse was a major annexation policy used by the British in India
It was actively implemented during the rule of Lord Dalhousie
It allowed British to annex states without a natural heir
Annexation of Oudh was one of the most controversial actions of British policy
These policies increased resentment among Indian rulers and contributed to 1857 revolt

notes.heading: Doctrine of Lapse – Introduction
points: Introduced and systematically applied by Lord Dalhousie (Governor-General 1848–1856)
Applied to princely states under British subsidiary system
If a ruler died without a natural male heir, state would 'lapse' to British
Adopted sons were not recognized as legal heirs unless approved by British
Used as legal justification for annexation

notes.heading: Conditions of Doctrine of Lapse
points: No natural male heir = state annexation
Adopted heir not automatically recognized
British approval required for adoption legitimacy
Ruler had to be loyal under subsidiary alliance system
Failure of compliance led to annexation

notes.heading: States Annexed under Doctrine of Lapse
points: Satara (1848) – first state annexed
Jaitpur and Sambalpur
Baghat
Jhansi (1853) – most famous case
Nagpur (1854)
Udaipur (partially affected)

notes.heading: Significance of Doctrine of Lapse
points: Expanded British territorial control rapidly
Undermined traditional rights of Indian rulers
Created fear and insecurity among princely states
Increased resentment against British rule
One of the political causes of Revolt of 1857

notes.heading: Criticism of Doctrine of Lapse
points: Violated Indian traditions of adoption
Seen as unethical and aggressive expansion policy
Destroyed legitimacy of native rulers
Encouraged distrust towards British intentions
Contributed to political instability in India

notes.heading: Annexation of Oudh – Background
points: Oudh (Awadh) was one of the richest provinces in India
Ruled by Nawabs under British subsidiary alliance
British interference increased over time
Allegations of misgovernance used as justification
Key strategic and economic importance for British

notes.heading: Annexation of Oudh – Events
points: Lord Dalhousie accused Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of misrule
British Resident influenced administration heavily
In 1856, Oudh was annexed on grounds of 'administrative failure'
Nawab was deposed and pensioned off
State came under direct British control

notes.heading: Significance of Annexation of Oudh
points: Created widespread resentment among nobility and soldiers (sepoys)
Many sepoys of Bengal army came from Oudh region
Increased anger against British policies
Contributed directly to outbreak of Revolt of 1857
Strengthened British control over North India

notes.heading: Comparison: Doctrine of Lapse vs Annexation of Oudh
points: Doctrine of Lapse based on succession issues
Annexation of Oudh based on alleged misrule
Both used as justification for expansion
Both led to political dissatisfaction among Indians
Both were policies of Lord Dalhousie

notes.heading: Role of Lord Dalhousie
points: Governor-General of India (1848–1856)
Implemented aggressive expansion policies
Introduced Doctrine of Lapse
Annexed key states including Punjab, Oudh (indirectly via policy framework)
Strengthened British administrative control in India

notes.heading: Impact on Indian Society and Politics
points: Disruption of traditional princely system
Loss of political autonomy for Indian rulers
Increased dissatisfaction among military and civilian population
Strengthened anti-British sentiments
Set stage for 1857 revolt

notes.heading: Historical Significance
points: Doctrine of Lapse marked peak of British annexation policy
Annexation of Oudh became symbol of British exploitation
Both policies accelerated collapse of Indian princely autonomy
Contributed significantly to 1857 Revolt
Shifted India towards direct Crown rule after 1858
